title: World Religions Paper 1 Revision: Practical Guide
summary: World religions paper 1 revision made practical: learn the current format, stimulus strategy, timing, and a worked example for confident IB exam prep.
body_markdown:
World religions paper 1 revision becomes much simpler once you understand what the examination is really testing. You need accurate religious knowledge, but knowledge alone is not enough. You must interpret a stimulus, follow the command term and select evidence that answers the precise question.


There is also an important format update. The familiar format used in older course materials was five 10-mark stimulus questions, each divided into 3 and 7 marks, completed in 1 hour 15 minutes. Current official materials for the May 2026 examination show that each question is now worth 9 marks, with the extended part reduced from 7 to 6 marks. The examination still requires five answers in 1 hour 15 minutes. Confirm the format for your session with your teacher and the current IB subject documentation before practising.


The central strategy remains unchanged: know several religions securely, read every stimulus purposefully and build concise answers around relevant evidence.


### Paper 1 revision checklist


Before the IB World Religions exam, make sure you can:


- explain the current structure for your examination session
- identify the strongest five questions while meeting the section rules
- connect unfamiliar stimuli to beliefs, practices, texts and experiences
- distinguish a short 3-mark response from an extended 6-mark or legacy 7-mark response
- answer the command term rather than writing everything you remember
- complete five responses within 75 minutes
- review mistakes using markschemes, feedback and targeted retrieval


The[RevisionDojo IB World Religions resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions) brings together syllabus-aligned Study Notes, Flashcards, videos and exam-style practice for this process.


### Understand the World Religions Paper 1 format


Paper 1 contains nine stimulus questions, one for each religion in the introductory part of the course. They are arranged into three sections:


Section Religions


A Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism


B Judaism, Christianity and Islam


C Taoism, Jainism and the Baha'i Faith


You answer five questions in total and must select at least one from each section. In practical terms, that means choosing one question from every section, then taking your remaining two from whichever religions offer your strongest combination of knowledge and stimulus understanding.


Version of the format Marks per question Total marks Time


Legacy materials 3 + 7 50 1 hour 15 minutes


Current 2026 materials 3 + 6 45 1 hour 15 minutes


This distinction matters when using older worksheets or school resources. A legacy 7-mark answer normally needs slightly more development than the current 6-mark part, but both reward the same fundamental qualities: focus, accurate knowledge, clear explanation and effective use of the stimulus.


Because assessment arrangements can change, use the version assigned to your examination session. Do not assume that an older practice booklet defines your current mark allocation.


### Build knowledge around examinable connections


A common revision mistake is treating each religion as a long list of terms. Lists feel safe because they are easy to highlight. Yet Paper 1 stimulus questions rarely reward isolated vocabulary. They reward connections.


For each religion, organise your notes around five questions:


- What does the tradition teach about ultimate reality or the sacred?
- How do those beliefs shape worship and conduct?
- Which texts, figures or narratives support them?
- How might followers experience these ideas in daily life?
- What distinctions exist within the tradition?


Take Buddhist impermanence as an example. Knowing the term *anicca* is useful. A stronger understanding connects impermanence to attachment, suffering, meditation and the way a Buddhist might respond to change. That network gives you several routes into an unfamiliar stimulus.


Use concise[World Religions Study Notes and practice resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions) to repair gaps, then convert the important relationships into Flashcards. The objective is not to copy paragraphs onto cards. Ask questions such as, “How does belief X influence practice Y?” This applies the principles in RevisionDojo’s guide to[active recall for IB revision](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/active-recall-ib-revision) .


### Read Paper 1 stimulus questions actively


The stimulus is not decoration. It tells you where to aim.


Read the question before reading the passage, image or extract in detail. Underline the command term, identify the named religion and notice the concept being tested. Then annotate the stimulus with no more than three useful observations.


A reliable reading sequence is:


1. Identify exactly what the question asks.
2. Locate a detail in the stimulus that relates to it.
3. Recall the religious concept behind that detail.
4. Decide which supporting example will make the explanation precise.


This prevents a subtle but expensive error: describing the stimulus without explaining its religious significance. If an image contains a ritual object, naming the object is only the beginning. Explain how it functions, what belief it expresses and why it matters to practitioners.


A student brings an enormous suitcase of knowledge while an invigilator reminds them that the question asks for one relevant thing


*The challenge is rarely having nothing to say. It is choosing what the question actually needs.*


### Match your answer to the marks


A 3-mark part should be brief, direct and visibly divided into creditworthy ideas. Depending on the wording, that may mean three accurate points or fewer points with explanation. Let the command term guide the structure and avoid turning a short response into an essay.


For the extended 6-mark or legacy 7-mark part, use a simple sequence:


- make a focused claim
- support it with accurate religious knowledge
- connect it to the stimulus
- explain its significance
- add a distinct second development where appropriate


Do not mechanically repeat the passage. A stimulus reference gains value when you interpret it. Likewise, do not attach memorised knowledge that has no clear relationship to the prompt.


RevisionDojo’s[IB Questionbank and exam-style practice](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/questionbank) can help you practise this selection process. After each response, use grading tools or AI Chat to identify missing explanation, unclear terminology and unsupported claims. Feedback should lead to one specific correction, not merely a score.


### A short worked example


Consider this constructed practice stimulus:


> A Buddhist practitioner observes a flower beginning to fade and reflects that attachment to changing things creates distress.


Suppose part (a) asks: **Identify three Buddhist ideas suggested by the stimulus.**


A concise 3-mark response could be:


- The fading flower illustrates *anicca* , the impermanence of conditioned things.
- The distress caused by attachment relates to *dukkha* .
- Recognising and loosening attachment connects to the path towards liberation from suffering.


Each point answers the task directly. There is no long introduction and no unnecessary history.


Suppose part (b) asks: **Explain how the stimulus reflects Buddhist teachings about suffering.**


A developed response might begin:


> The fading flower reflects *anicca* , because its beauty and physical form cannot remain permanent. The practitioner’s distress does not arise simply because the flower changes, but because of attachment to its previous condition. This connects the stimulus to *dukkha* and to the teaching that craving contributes to suffering. By recognising change without clinging to it, a Buddhist practitioner can cultivate wisdom and reduce attachment. The reflection therefore turns an ordinary experience into an opportunity to understand the causes of suffering and practise a more detached response.


This answer works because every sentence advances the explanation. It identifies doctrine, interprets the stimulus and shows practical significance. To strengthen a longer legacy 7-mark version, you might add a carefully explained connection to the Four Noble Truths or Buddhist practice, provided it remains relevant.


### Manage the 75 minutes deliberately


Five answers in 75 minutes gives you an average of 15 minutes per question. A practical plan is:


Task Suggested time per question


Read, choose and annotate 1-2 minutes


Complete the 3-mark part 3-4 minutes


Complete the extended part 8-9 minutes


Check relevance and terminology 1 minute


Use the opening minutes to scan all nine options and mark your strongest five while checking that you have represented Sections A, B and C. Avoid choosing purely because you recognise the stimulus. Choose questions for which you can explain the underlying religious content.


Practise this under realistic conditions with[RevisionDojo’s World Religions mock exam preparation guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-world-religions-mock-exam-prep-november) . Predicted Papers and Mock Exams can make timing feel ordinary before the real examination, while Tutors can help diagnose recurring issues in interpretation or structure.


### Use a revision cycle that produces evidence


Reading creates familiarity, and familiarity can masquerade as readiness. A better weekly cycle moves from recall to application:


- **Day 1:** Retrieve beliefs and practices from memory.
- **Day 2:** Review weak areas with Study Notes.
- **Day 3:** Answer two untimed stimulus questions.
- **Day 4:** Check the responses and rewrite one weak paragraph.
- **Day 5:** Complete five questions under the 75-minute limit.
- **Day 6:** Turn mistakes into Flashcards or AI Chat prompts.
- **Day 7:** Rest or complete a short retrieval session.


RevisionDojo’s explanation of[spaced repetition for IB revision](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/spaced-repetition-ib-revision) can help you revisit difficult material before it fades. The[IB Flashcard active-recall system](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-flashcard-system-active-recall-for-better-memory) is particularly useful for terms, sacred texts, founders, practices and doctrinal relationships.


Keep an error log with three columns: what went wrong, why it happened and what you will do next. “Weak Buddhism” is too vague. “I described meditation without connecting it to the reduction of attachment” gives you something concrete to repair.


### Revise respectfully and precisely


World religions answers can lose clarity when they make absolute statements about diverse traditions. Avoid phrases suggesting that every follower believes or practises in exactly the same way. Where relevant, distinguish between schools, denominations or interpretations.


Precision also means using religious terminology accurately rather than adding specialised vocabulary for appearance. RevisionDojo’s guide to[common World Religions misconceptions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-world-religions-misconceptions) can help you identify oversimplifications before they enter timed answers.


The best preparation gradually narrows the distance between what you know and what you can use. RevisionDojo supports that journey in one place through its Questionbank, Study Notes, Flashcards, AI Chat, grading tools, Predicted Papers, Mock Exams, Coursework Library and Tutors. For Paper 1, the essential combination is simple: retrieve accurate knowledge, apply it to fresh stimuli, receive feedback and try again. Calmness usually arrives after the process becomes familiar.
